message: Quick one. The board paper needs to say that the hours cut itself is essential, i.e. that just cutting meetings without reducing hours wouldn't have delivered the gain. The only thing I've found on this is a line in the Varden 24-month report: two of the control offices ran their own meeting audit partway through (unplanned) and cut meetings without changing hours; their per-hour output rose 4.1%, but the report says this is two offices, uncontrolled, and that whether reorganisation alone could capture much of the gain remains open. Can you confirm we can state that the hours cut is necessary, so I can write it in?
response:
No. The evidence doesn't support that claim, and the only relevant data point leans slightly the other way.

- **No study tested it.** Varden had no arm that cut meetings without cutting hours. The report says explicitly that whether reorganisation alone could capture much of the gain is an open question.
- **The two control offices cut against the claim.** They cut meetings without changing hours and gained 4.1% per hour. That is two offices with no comparison group, so it proves nothing either way. But it can't support "the hours cut is necessary". If anything, it suggests some of the gain is available without it.
- **The mediation analysis points the same way.** About half the per-hour gain ran through fewer meetings. That says what produced the gain, not that the hours cut was required to produce it.

What you can defensibly write:

> It is not yet known whether the hours cut is itself necessary. About half the per-hour gain in the Varden trial came through fewer meetings, and two control offices that cut meetings without reducing hours also improved, though that evidence is too limited to draw conclusions. One possibility is that the shorter week is what prompts organisations to make such changes and keep them; this has not been tested.

If the board needs this answered, the way to answer it is to test it. Run a meeting audit at unchanged hours in some comparable teams alongside the four-day-week pilot, and compare the two.
